recent_posts.title: How to manage high amplitude disagreeableness in startup teams
recent_posts.summary: Startup people share a distinctive trait called 'high amplitude disagreeableness' — they may not argue constantly, but when they do, they go all-in, publicly and persistently. This stems from a creator mindset rather than an extractor mindset. Managers who want to attract and retain entrepreneurial talent need to match that intensity themselves, build cultures that tolerate strong disagreement without punishment, and avoid being confidently wrong — because startup people will remember and hold it against you.

recent_posts.title: Management In The Age Of AI
recent_posts.summary: AI tools reached an inflection point in late 2025, fundamentally changing what good management looks like. Managers in 2026 must become hands-on builders to understand AI tooling firsthand, raise output expectations since powerful tools eliminate many old excuses, actively manage AI spend as pricing shifts to consumption-based models, enforce precise goal clarity to avoid building the wrong things fast, and deliberately force team collaboration as everyone works heads-down with personal agent fleets. Hiring standards must also rise sharply, as the gap between great and mediocre engineers amplified by AI tools is now roughly 100x rather than 2x.

recent_posts.title: Avoiding a Culture of Emergencies
recent_posts.summary: Well-managed teams experience far fewer emergencies than poorly managed ones. Four key practices separate good managers from bad: staying deeply informed about what their teams actually do, maintaining strong conviction about what work truly matters so they can push back on unnecessary requests, building a mental model of the team and business to anticipate future needs, and genuinely caring about team well-being. Emergencies are often a choice — the result of managers prioritizing short-term convenience over their team's long-term productivity. Reducing emergencies leads to happier teams, better retention, and the focused environment that great work requires.

recent_posts.title: Why engineering and sales are the only critical teams in B2B software
recent_posts.summary: In B2B software companies, engineering and sales are the only truly critical functions because they directly build and sell the product. All other roles, including product management, design, and marketing, exist to support these two core teams. This reality has important implications: non-engineering/sales teams must recognize their supporting role and prioritize these functions' needs, sales and engineering leaders face intense pressure to continuously improve or risk replacement, and adjacent roles should deeply understand these disciplines to be effective. The prominence of engineering and sales explains why tech CEOs often come from these backgrounds, why product-led growth can succeed by eliminating sales risk, and why investors like Y Combinator require engineering expertise on founding teams.

recent_posts.title: Advice For Individual Contributors
recent_posts.summary: Individual contributors can achieve outsized impact by making breakthroughs through intense focused work, acting as unbiased leaders rather than union reps, taking specific ownership of goals, sending regular bi-weekly updates to management, and proactively engaging with senior leaders to solve their problems. The key is leveraging the IC's ability to execute quickly while building visibility and relationships across the organization.

recent_posts.title: Senior engineers and PMs should own key metrics as graphs
recent_posts.summary: Senior engineers, PMs, and designers should own at least one key metric visualized as a graph to demonstrate impact and communicate effectively. Graphs provide concise communication of progress on important problems like performance, cost reduction, or revenue growth, replacing lengthy explanations with clear visual data. This practice helps track progress, articulate value to leadership, receive actionable feedback, and advance careers by making contributions visible and measurable.

recent_posts.title: The Two Jobs of a CPO
recent_posts.summary: Chief Product Officers face two distinct responsibilities: building strong product culture and processes within their teams, and maintaining strategic alignment with the CEO on product direction. While product culture can be improved iteratively, strategic alignment is critical from day one and non-negotiable. The role requires balancing operational excellence through delegation and templates with hands-on strategic direction that cannot be delegated. Success depends on hiring people who understand the company's strategic direction, establishing efficient product operations, and maintaining constant communication with the CEO to ensure both jobs are accomplished effectively.

recent_posts.title: Leveling Up Teams Fast and Slow
recent_posts.summary: Two fundamental strategies for building high-performing teams: systematically improving your weakest team to raise the organizational baseline (slow approach), and empowering your most competent people to lead critical projects regardless of hierarchy (fast approach). The slow method prevents organizational degradation by continuously debugging underperforming teams one at a time. The fast method leverages top performers as singular leaders on complex projects, which works better than committee-style leadership and delivers immediate results despite potential political friction.

recent_posts.title: The hidden costs of specialization in growing engineering teams
recent_posts.summary: Growing companies face a critical tradeoff when transitioning from generalists to specialists. While specialization improves output quality, it dramatically increases coordination costs, slows delivery, and raises the probability of underperforming team members blocking progress. Exceptional generalists often outperform average specialists in adjacent domains. To mitigate these risks, companies should stay lean with minimal org layers, maintain strong project oversight, and develop processes to quickly detect and address performance issues.
